_source: Schmersal AZM 161CC-12/03RKA-024 safety interlock, recorded product page (1.2 MB). Values VERIFIED against the page: `IP67` appears 9×, `24 VAC/DC` 14×, `cULus`, `Ambient temperature`, the material string `glass-fibre reinforced thermoplastic`, and `419` (the weight) inside the page's embedded JSON. The specs live in a JSON blob rather than DOM tables — which is why this page is the one that exposed HTML markup leaking into attribute names.
_tier: value-verified. The richest HTML fixture in the corpus: proper IEC labels (Uimp, Ui, utilisation categories AC-15/DC-13), so it guards the generic path's best-case behaviour.

_notes.html_markup: This fixture found P1.3c: attributes arrived as `Rated impulse withstand voltage U<sub>imp</sub>` and `Rated insulation voltage U<sub>i</sub>` — markup inside the attribute NAME, so the Excel export would have shown it literally. Grepping the HTML for `<sub>` finds nothing: the tags exist only inside the embedded JSON, whose strings never pass through cheerio's text extraction. The mustNotContain entries above pin the fix.
_notes.storage_vs_operating: The page states BOTH `Ambient temperature -30 ... +60 °C` and `Storage and transport temperature -30 ... +85 °C`. operatingTemperatureMax must be 60, never 85 — so this fixture also guards the storage-temperature exclusion in deriveOperatingTemperature.
_notes.why_this_one: Chosen for promotion because its yield looked suspiciously low for a 1.2 MB page. It was not low — 45 attributes and 9 normalized fields is a clean read — but checking that assumption is what surfaced the markup bug.
